id: A Lullaby, for the Fir Tree Growing in My Left Lung

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: All, Senate, The

outputs.L1:
All we know of history  
we learn from scenes in the mosaic of bone  
on the Senate floor:

The Flood makes graves of the fields,  
and the angels harvest enough suffering  
to live for another thousand years.

Moses pulls off his beard and lights a cigarette.  
*I’m tired of pretending.*

He pushes his box of spare commandments under his bed,  
and as he drifts to sleep, his eyes, like caves,  
fill with paintings of woolly rhinos.

Sailing ships forest a small island.  
One light shines from a caravel—the captain’s quarters.  
It’s Christopher Columbus.

All night he’s been sewing shrouds  
as arrival gifts for the natives.

Little Chris presses his bleeding fingers to his mouth  
and cries quietly, *No one appreciates me.*

God and the devil tuck him into bed.  
*It’ll get better,* they say.

Together they complete the shrouds for him  
while he dreams of golden nipples.

As it was, it is now.

Spring translates the earth into hope—  
tongues of grass taste the sea salt on the west wind  
and the blood on soldiers’ boots.

This morning, one of the old poets—  
unkillable cockroach—cycled past me, yelling,  
*You have the brightest light in America! Ha ha!*

On my dresser, a spider makes a web  
along the contours of my bra.

We lie on the bed together;  
I run my hand up the muscles of your leg  
and feel its eons of evolution,  
now outlawed by the Senate.
outputs.L2:
Everything we understand about the past  
comes from tableaux set in the Senate chamber’s bone mosaic:

The deluge turns farmland into burial ground,  
and angels gather so much misery  
they can survive on it for another millennium.

Moses tears away his beard, strikes a match,  
and smokes. He says he can’t keep up the charade.  
He slides a carton of backup laws beneath the bed,  
then falls asleep. His cavernous eyes  
crowd with images of shaggy rhinoceroses.

A tiny island bristles with the masts of ships.  
A lone lamp burns aboard one caravel, in the captain’s room.  
Columbus is inside.

He has spent the entire night stitching burial cloths  
to present to the Indigenous people when he lands.  
Young Christopher puts his cut fingers between his lips  
and softly weeps that nobody values him.

The deity and the demon settle him beneath the covers,  
promising that things will improve.  
Working side by side, they finish the winding sheets  
as he sleeps and imagines nipples made of gold.

What happened before continues to happen.

Spring renders the ground in the language of optimism:  
blades of grass sample the ocean brine carried by the western breeze  
and the gore clinging to military boots.

Earlier today, an aging poet—  
indestructible as a roach—rode a bicycle past me, shouting,  
“Your light outshines every other light in the nation!”  
Then he laughed.

A spider on my bureau spins silk  
following the shape of my brassiere.

We stretch out beside each other on the mattress.  
My palm travels over the strength of your leg,  
sensing the vast ages that formed it through evolution—  
a process the Senate has now forbidden.
outputs.L3:
The poem portrays history not as a coherent story of progress, but as a fragmented mosaic made up of violence, suffering, myth, and political power. Historical and religious figures appear in unfamiliar, unsettling forms that challenge traditional heroic narratives. Moses, for example, seems exhausted by religious pretense. Rather than confidently presenting divine law, he hides his commandments and dreams of escaping into prehistoric life, before organized religion and its burdens existed.

Christopher Columbus is treated with even sharper irony. He prepares death and destruction for Indigenous people while imagining himself to be misunderstood and insufficiently appreciated. His mission appears to receive support from both divine and demonic forces, blurring the distinction between sacred purpose and evil. Through this portrayal, the poem exposes how conquest and brutality have often been justified through religion, destiny, and self-glorifying myths.

These historical images are not confined to the distant past. The poem suggests that earlier forms of cruelty continue to shape the present, particularly through institutions and political authority. Nevertheless, images of spring introduce the possibility of hope, renewal, and resistance. Against the weight of inherited violence, the natural world continues to regenerate.

The poem finally contrasts personal intimacy and the vast history of human evolution with political forces represented by the Senate. Love, desire, and embodied human connection are presented as ancient and natural, while political institutions attempt to deny, regulate, or outlaw them. This contrast reveals the absurdity of using temporary systems of power to suppress experiences rooted deeply in human life. The poem therefore holds brutality and renewal in tension, suggesting that although the past remains painfully present, intimacy, nature, and hope still offer forms of endurance.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents history not as a steady movement toward justice, but as a cycle in which violence, conquest, and political repression repeatedly return. Its surreal imagery brings together biblical figures, Columbus, warfare, the natural world, and moments of private intimacy, collapsing the boundaries between distant eras and personal experience. These unexpected juxtapositions suggest that the forces shaping ancient stories and colonial expansion remain active in the present. The refrain “as it was” reinforces this sense of repetition: suffering survives beneath claims of progress, while power continues to disguise cruelty as faith, civilization, patriotism, or historical necessity.

By placing Columbus alongside sacred and contemporary images, the poem challenges heroic versions of colonial history. Exploration cannot be separated from invasion, displacement, and the suppression of other peoples’ memories. Similarly, biblical language is not treated as purely consoling or morally authoritative. Instead, it exposes the distance between professed spiritual ideals and the hypocrisy of institutions that justify domination. Religion, politics, and official history all risk becoming instruments of repression when they deny violence or present it as inevitable.

War also enters the poem as both a public catastrophe and an intimate wound. Political conflict affects bodies, relationships, landscapes, and everyday life; it is never merely an abstract event recorded in textbooks. The poem’s shifts between collective history and private experience show how large systems of power penetrate ordinary existence. Distorted historical memory deepens this harm by erasing victims, simplifying the past, and preventing society from recognizing recurring patterns of oppression.

Yet the poem does not remain entirely trapped in despair. Nature, especially the arrival or promise of spring, introduces a different kind of recurrence. Unlike the repetition implied by “as it was,” spring represents renewal, growth, and the possibility of transformation. The natural world resists doctrines and institutions that attempt to deny change, history, or evolution. Its cycles reveal that life persists even after devastation.

Embodied love and artistic creation offer similar forms of resistance. Physical intimacy affirms vulnerability, connection, and the reality of the living body against political systems that reduce people to symbols, enemies, or historical abstractions. Art preserves what official narratives try to erase and creates new relationships among fragments of experience. Through imagination, the poem confronts inherited violence without surrendering to it.

Ultimately, the poem holds repetition and renewal in tension. Human beings continue to reproduce conquest, repression, and hypocrisy “as it was,” but this is not the only pattern available. Love, art, memory, and spring embody a resilient hope: not a naïve belief that suffering will disappear, but a determination to remain alive, truthful, and capable of change despite institutions that deny both history and evolution.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem that blends biblical figures, Columbus, prehistory, political satire, intimacy, and cyclical violence, ending with evolution being outlawed by the Senate.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn, Noah counted the senators  
two by two,  
their polished shoes still wet  
from a flood they had voted against.

Eve slept beneath a billboard  
advertising innocence.  
Adam, ashamed of his ribs,  
filed them into little white fences  
and called the enclosure history.

Across the parking lot  
Columbus steered three shopping carts west,  
each piled with compasses  
pointing toward somebody else’s home.  
He planted a flag in the produce aisle,  
renamed the oranges,  
and demanded a holiday.

Under the linoleum,  
a trilobite dreamed of ballots.  
A mammoth dragged its tusks  
through the red tape of winter.  
In a cave, our ancestors pressed  
their bloody palms to stone—  
the first signatures  
on the first petition  
the king would never read.

You and I lay close  
while the republic sharpened its teeth.  
Your breath moved over my shoulder  
like a small animal crossing moonlight.  
I whispered your name  
into the ancient cup of your ear,  
and for one ungoverned moment  
the armies forgot which century  
they were supposed to burn.

Then Cain rose again,  
wearing Abel’s campaign button.  
David loaded the sling  
with a televised apology.  
Goliath purchased the network.  
The prophets were thanked for their service  
and escorted from the chamber.

Every sword came back as a plowshare,  
every plowshare as a bayonet,  
every bayonet as a fountain pen  
signing the children into battle.  
The wheel turned.  
The wound learned the wheel.  
The wheel learned applause.

At noon, dinosaurs entered the Capitol  
in powdered wigs,  
their fossils humming beneath the marble.  
They debated whether fire was natural,  
whether stars required permits,  
whether the human heart  
had been properly peer-reviewed.

Outside, Noah’s rain began again.  
Columbus claimed it.  
Eve bit the microphone.  
You took my hand beneath the table  
as if tenderness were contraband.

And by evening, evolution was outlawed by the Senate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental prose poem in which Moses smokes, Christopher Columbus sews shrouds for Indigenous people, God and the devil comfort him, and the speaker reflects on love and America.
counterfactuals.output:
Moses smokes at the edge of the promised country, tapping ash from the commandments as if every law contains a small fire and every fire an exhausted law. The desert enters his lungs. He calls it history. He calls it nothing.

Across the water, Christopher Columbus sits beneath a torn flag, sewing shrouds for the Indigenous dead. His needle is a narrow mast. His thread, a red meridian. He cannot finish: each body becomes a nation; each nation rises and removes its stolen name. Still he sews—empire’s little domestic gesture—while the ships rot backward into trees.

God rests one hand on his shoulder. The devil rests the other.

There, there, they say.

But comfort is not forgiveness. Even heaven knows this. Even hell.

I have loved America the way one loves a house built over voices: sleeplessly, listening at the pipes. I have loved its highways, its borrowed hymns, its orchards planted in wounds. I have loved people here—not the map’s hard fist, not the anthem scrubbing blood from its mouth, but the people passing bread through the smoke.

Moses offers me a cigarette. I refuse, then take it. The ember glows like a minor revelation.

What is love, if not the refusal to call conquest destiny? What is America, if not a sentence still arguing with its first word?

Behind us, the dead unwrap themselves.

Ahead, no promised land—

only land,

and the difficult promise  
to belong to it without possession.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly comic, dreamlike poem about how history is preserved in bones and repeated through religion, colonialism, war, and contemporary politics. Use vivid anachronisms and startling imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Department of Reoccurring Weather**

In the museum basement, the bones are voting.  
A femur checks the wrong box on purpose.  
A skull, still wearing its empire like a hat,  
demands a recount from the dust.

History sleeps badly in the calcium.  
At midnight it grinds its teeth—  
Jericho, Calcutta, Verdun—  
and wakes with a mouthful of flags.

The saints arrive in Roman sandals  
and campaign hoodies, streaming live  
from the tasteful ruins. One blesses the cannon.  
One canonizes the algorithm.  
One sells tiny wooden crosses  
with free international shipping.

Outside, Columbus circles a parking garage,  
unable to find the New World.  
His compass points to the gift shop.  
The gift shop points to the sugar fields.  
The sugar fields, politely rebranded,  
point to a shareholder meeting  
where the ghosts applaud quarterly growth.

Napoleon rides a drone over Waterloo.  
Caesar updates his terms of service.  
The Mongol horde waits at customs  
while an officer asks whether conquest  
is business or pleasure.

In the chapel, war kneels down  
to pray to itself.

It has many names and excellent posture.  
It wears a poppy, a medal, a necktie,  
a child’s red mitten on one antenna.  
It whispers *peace* into the microphone  
until the microphone catches fire.

The bones remember every sermon  
delivered above a mass grave.  
They remember the missionary’s soap,  
the governor’s map, the soldier’s joke,  
the clean white margins of the textbook  
where the missing learned to live.

Now Parliament floats through my bedroom  
on the back of a dead whale.  
The ministers debate which century this is.  
One says the twelfth. One says the market.  
One peels an orange with a bayonet  
and calls the spray collateral sunlight.

Meanwhile, the old gods work night shifts  
moderating comments.  
They delete blasphemy, irony, evidence.  
They issue blue checks to the horsemen,  
who have traded their horses for scooters  
and complain the apocalypse  
has no dedicated parking.

At dawn, archaeologists open the earth  
like a badly addressed letter.

Dear Future,  
the skeletons have written,  
we tried everything again.

Please find enclosed:  
one crown, two bullets,  
a ballot with blood in its little mouth,  
and the sacred recipe for forgetting.

But the bones do not forget.

They lie beneath cathedrals and pipelines,  
under podiums, palaces, border walls,  
quiet as cutlery before dinner—  
each rib a curved white calendar,  
each jaw still rehearsing the punchline.

And when history finally walks onstage,  
wearing a judge’s wig and a clown’s shoes,  
we laugh because it is ridiculous.

We laugh because it is armed.

We laugh because the skull  
at the ballot box  
has our name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary American poem with no stanza breaks, featuring the Flood, angels harvesting suffering, cave paintings of woolly rhinos, ships surrounding an island, an eccentric old poet on a bicycle, and a spider weaving over a bra.
counterfactuals.output: After the Flood, we found the strip malls shining under ten feet of water, / their red signs wavering like wounds nobody could close. / Angels came in work gloves, harvesting suffering / from rooftops, hospital corridors, the soaked back seats of cars, / bundling it into sheaves that hummed beneath their wings. / In a cave above the interstate, children drew woolly rhinos / in charcoal, broad-backed and running toward extinction / as if extinction were a country with better weather. / All night, ships surrounded the island—tankers, destroyers, / cruise liners lit like casinos—while the island kept / its one dark house, its one radio repeating Stay calm. / At dawn, an eccentric old poet pedaled past the barricades, / bicycle basket full of peaches and unpaid bills, / shouting that America was still an unfinished sentence. / Nobody argued. We were tired of grammar, tired of rescue, / tired of watching the sky rehearse its ancient anger. / In an upstairs bedroom, abandoned in the hurry, / a spider wove her silver republic over a bra, / fastening cup to cup with bridges finer than mercy. / The water climbed. The angels bent to their labor. / The rhinos ran beneath our feet, black and immense, / and the old poet rang his little bell at every locked door / as if someone, somewhere, might still answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a lyrical surrealist monologue that moves from the Senate floor through biblical and colonial history into a bedroom scene, contrasting springtime hope and erotic tenderness with bloodshed, censorship, and anti-evolution politics.
counterfactuals.output:
I rise on the Senate floor with pollen in my pockets.

Above me, the chandeliers tremble like captive constellations, and every polished desk has learned to resemble a coffin. The clerk calls the roll; the names fall one by one into a silver bowl. Yea. Nay. Yea. Nay. Two small oars rowing the republic backward.

Outside, spring has broken the seal of winter. Magnolias lift their pale petitions. Sparrows conduct their riotous committees in the gutters. Even the marble heroes, greened by weather, seem to loosen their stone collars and breathe.

But inside, a senator holds up a book with half its pages blackened.

He says: This is for the children.

Another produces a vial of blood and calls it history.

Another says the earth is young, younger than grief, younger than the fossils sleeping under our highways. He would have the trilobite recant, the whale return its legs, the ape apologize for our resemblance. He bangs the gavel, and somewhere a museum darkens its oldest room.

I want to tell them that God did not fear the dark.

In the beginning, darkness was not contraband. It lay upon the face of the deep, immense and unedited, while the spirit moved over the waters like a hand searching for another hand in sleep. Then light arrived—not as a policeman, not as a censor’s blade, but as astonishment.

Yet Cain raises his stone again in every century. Abel keeps falling through the tall grass, his blood inventing red alphabets in the soil. Noah shuts the door against the drowning multitude. Abraham wakes with a knife gleaming above the beloved body. Lot’s wife turns, because love must look back, and history punishes her with salt.

We have eaten that salt ever since.

It glittered on the lips of conquistadors kneeling before gold. It crusted the ropes of slave ships. It whitened the maps where empires drew straight borders through villages, rivers, languages, and the migratory dreams of animals. Men arrived carrying crosses, muskets, ledgers. They measured the land, renamed the mountains, outlawed the drums, and taught the dead to answer to foreign names.

At night they wrote home about providence.

At dawn the orchards were burning.

The Senate murmurs beneath its painted ceiling. Someone strikes the word *body* from a schoolbook. Someone strikes *desire*. Someone strikes *enslaved* and writes *worker*. Someone removes the kiss, the wound, the question. The wastebaskets fill with forbidden moons.

Still, spring presses its green mouth to every locked door.

And then I am no longer speaking beneath the dome.

I am in our bedroom, where evening has unbuttoned the windows. Rain breathes against the screen. Your dress lies over the chair like a flag after surrender, and your bare shoulder holds a small republic of lamplight.

Come closer.

Let the lawmakers debate whether we descended from stars or mud. I have evidence: the soft animal of your breathing, the ancient hinge of your knee, the salt at your throat. I touch you gently, as though the world were not conquered territory. You touch me as though no scripture had ever been sharpened into a weapon.

Between us, tenderness begins its dangerous curriculum.

Your fingers move along my spine, counting the vertebrae the censors deny. Millions of years flower beneath your palm. The first fish stirs in its dark water; the first wing opens; the first creature crawls from the sea and dreams, impossibly, of bedsheets, thunder, and the beloved.

Outside, sirens braid themselves through the rain.

Somewhere a child closes a banned book and keeps its bright animal alive behind the ribs. Somewhere a soldier washes blood from his hands and cannot wash away the hands. Somewhere a statue of an admiral points forever toward a country he mistook for emptiness.

But here, for one ungoverned hour, your mouth meets mine.

No empire enters.

No gavel falls.

The room fills with the scent of wet earth and the reckless white blossoms of the pear tree. I hear the future scratching softly inside the walls—not a doctrine, not a flag, but a green and many-legged thing, changing because it must, surviving because it can.

Tomorrow they may return with scissors for the tongue, with fire for the library, with laws denying the long patience of bone.

Tonight, beloved, let us be older than their fear.

Let us lie down in the unfinished garden, tender and temporary, while spring rehearses its uprising under every grave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
